Psychology in film, literature and music

The man who mistook his wife for a hat

Oliver Sacks turned neurological cases into literature. One of them gave his most famous book its title.

In 1985, the neurologist Oliver Sacks published a book of clinical cases told as stories. The title story is that of "Dr P.", a music teacher who could see perfectly well but could not recognise what he saw: as he was leaving, he reached for his wife's head, thinking it was his hat.

Visual agnosia

Dr P. had visual agnosia, probably from a degenerative illness affecting the brain areas that interpret vision. He could describe the parts of a glove ("a continuous surface, infolded on itself, with five outpouchings") but did not know what it was. As soon as he touched it, he recognised it. He got by singing to himself while he dressed or ate.

Sacks wrote about many other conditions, such as prosopagnosia, which he had himself: difficulty recognising faces. His books brought neurology to a wide audience, although some criticised him for exposing vulnerable patients.

References

  1. Sacks, O. (1985). The Man Who Mistook His Wife for a Hat. Summit Books.
